name: Words, Wires and Waves
description: How people learned to send words and pictures farther and faster, from papyrus and the printing press to the telegraph, radio and television.

checkpoints.name: Reeds, paper and blocks
checkpoints.note: Egyptians wrote on papyrus, Chinese makers invented paper and woodblock printing, and Bi Sheng tried movable type. Messages still travelled only as fast as a runner or a horse.

checkpoints.name: The age of the press
checkpoints.note: Gutenberg’s press made books cheap and spread new ideas across Europe. France later built towers with signalling arms, the first national system for sending messages faster than a rider.

checkpoints.name: Wires across the world
checkpoints.note: The electric telegraph, Morse code, undersea cables and the telephone shrank distance. The postage stamp, photography and the phonograph also changed how people sent and kept news and sound.

checkpoints.name: Broadcasting begins
checkpoints.note: Radio carried voices into homes, and early television sent pictures. Films gained sound, and radio reached ships, armies and families in the same moment.

checkpoints.name: Screens and satellites
checkpoints.note: Colour television, satellites and glass fibre linked the planet. Records and discs gave recorded music a new home, and cables and signals carried images, voices and later the internet around the globe.
